newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans clamour for death penalty after rapes.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans clamour for death penalty after rapes.

text.p: South African Justice Minister Dullah Omar called on Tuesday for tough punishment to combat rape after a string of highly publicised cases, but resisted growing calls to bring back the death penalty.

The rapes of two pairs of young girls at luxury homes in the "crime capital" Johannesburg have helped focus attention on the issue in a society where it is usually overshadowed by rampant murder, violent attacks and armed car hijackings.

A rape is reported in South Africa every 14 minutes, around a third of them involving minors. Pressure groups say that means someone is violated every 30 seconds, based on a police guide that only one rape in 35 rape is ever reported.
Omar told a radio phone-in, replete with calls for vengeance from the public, that he was drafting legislation to bring in minimum sentences for violent crimes, among them rape.
"The death penalty is unconstitutional and it is out," he said. "State violence sets an example of violence and promotes a culture where violence is a part of life.
"The punishment must be serious, it must be felt, but it should not brutalise. Counter-brutalisation does not help," Omar said.

Opinion polls show about four-fifths of South Africans, terrified by life with some of the world's worst violent crime levels, want a return of capital punishment. It was last carried out in 1989 and was ruled unconstitutional in 1995.

"I want to kill them. They have destroyed my little girl," said the mother of a 15-year-old who, along with a younger cousin, lost her virginity in a gang rape last week while robbers tied up the rest of the family in their home.

"I would like changes in legislation to send a shudder through their spines, each one of them, whether it is a rapist at gunpoint or friendly uncle Joe down the road who is raping or the stepfather," she told television news.
President Nelson Mandela fiercely opposes the death penalty.
Suspected rapists and murderers are usually let out on bail by overburdened courts, another cause of protest.
Parents of two sisters aged 21 and 24, raped by a robbery gang last week, called for perpetrators to be castrated.

As with many crimes, it takes a famous or well-off -- which often means white -- victim to push the issue onto the agenda in a society which Omar said had become brutalised by violence, first political during the apartheid days and now criminal.
In some black townships, rape is so common that it is seen as an unfortunate fact of life, some anti-rape activists say.
Counsellors list the long-term effects: eating problems, mood swings, nightmares, frequent washing, lack of trust, fear of being alone, and relationship and sex problems.
Ordinary South Africans have started applauding vigilantes and other citizens who take the law into their own hands.
Messages of support flooded in when a policeman working with abused children, whose own six-year-old daughter was raped last week, went to the cells and gunned down the suspect.
One caller to Tuesday's phone-in, raped with her husband last month by robbers, sounded a rare note of conciliation.
"Four men came in with guns and screwdrivers. They tied us up and raped us. My husband later died of suffocation from the rope around his neck. We are pensioners," said Shirley.
"One rapist said, 'We have a black president and he can't help me get work, so this is how I live.' There must be some way we can give people employment to stop crime," she said.
